To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) for the Vertex Cover and the Independent Set problems, there are LCAs that use a number of WP probes that is linear in the maximum degree of the graph, and (2) for the Minimum Vertex Cover problem, there are LCAS that use a number WP probes that is logarithmic in the maximum degree.
the probe complexity of an LCA is determined by the number of distinct neighbors of the input graph.
(1) For the problem of computing a vertex cover, the best LCA that uses only SPs and WPs has a probe complexity of $\Omega(\Delta)$, where $\Delta$ is the maximum degree of the input graph.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: "What is the smallest number of probes that an LCA must make on graphs with arbitrarily high degrees?"
the following two questions: (i) How many probes are needed to compute a certain local output?
the following questions:  (i) Can the probe complexity of a problem in the LCA model be significantly improved by allowing the algorithm to make a small number of strong probes?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, for the problems studied here, the probe complexity of local computation algorithms is at most a constant times the probe complexity of the best possible local computation algorithms that can be used in the model.
for the problems considered, the probe complexity of local computation algorithms is at least as large as the maximum degree.

for any graph $G$ with maximum degree $n$ and minimum degree $d$ the probe complexity of an LCA that solves the vertex cover problem is $O(\log n \cdot d)$ for SPs and $\Omega(\frac{n}{\log d})$ for WPs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the LCA model can be very powerful: it can solve a wide variety of problems, including problems that are known to be computationally intractable.
, for a large number of problems, we show that the number of WP and SP probes made by an LCA is at most $O(\log \Delta)$, $O(\log^2 \Delta)$, and $O(\sqrt{\Delta})$, respectively.
we have found a number of problems for which the probe complexities of SP-LCAs and WP-LCAs are the same, and a number of problems where the complexities of SP-LCA and WP-LCA are different.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in contrast to what is known for the standard local model (in which the input graph is fully known), the probe complexity of the problem is not always determined by the maximum degree.
the complexity of LCAs is highly dependent on the number of weak probes allowed.

, in the SP+WP model, the number of probes required by LCAs to compute local outputs is determined by a parameter that we call the "local expansion", which is a local variant of the classical graph expansion parameter.
